title: SOLOMON LOVED MANY FOREIGN WOMEN—AND THE MOST FRIGHTENING PART IS THAT GOD HAD ALREADY WARNED HIM
paragraphs: SOLOMON LOVED MANY FOREIGN WOMEN—AND THE MOST FRIGHTENING PART IS THAT GOD HAD ALREADY WARNED HIM

He had wisdom that astonished nations, wealth beyond imagination, and a kingdom blessed by God. Yet the man who knew so much about God slowly gave his heart to what God had forbidden. This is not merely the tragedy of Solomon. It is a warning to every believer who knows the truth but keeps making exceptions for the one thing that could destroy them.
“But king Solomon loved many strange women…” — 1 Kings 11:1 (KJV)
There is something terrifying about a person who knows exactly what God has said… and still chooses to walk in the opposite direction.
Not because they have never heard the truth.
Not because nobody warned them.
Not because they lack spiritual knowledge.
But because somewhere between knowing God's Word and obeying it, something else has become more precious to them than surrender.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part of Solomon's story is this:
He did not begin as a man who hated God.
He began as a man who loved Him.
First Kings 3:3 tells us that Solomon loved the LORD and walked in the statutes of David his father, although his worship was not yet free from compromise.

He was the young king who confessed that he did not know how to govern God's people properly. When God appeared to him in a dream and invited him to ask for what he desired, Solomon did not ask for riches, revenge, or a longer life.
He asked for an understanding heart.
And God was pleased.
Imagine that.
A man who once asked God for wisdom would eventually become one of Scripture's most devastating examples of what happens when wisdom is separated from obedience.
How does someone go from building a temple for the glory of God to building places of worship for false gods?
How does a heart that once bowed before the LORD begin bowing before the idols of the nations?
And perhaps the question that should trouble us most is not, "How could Solomon do that?"
It is…
"Where am I doing the same thing?"
Because Solomon's downfall did not begin when he constructed an altar to an idol.
It began when he allowed his affections to negotiate with a command God had already made clear.
First Kings 11:1–2 records:
“But king Solomon loved many strange women, together with the daughter of Pharaoh, women of the Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Zidonians, and Hittites;

“Of the nations concerning which the LORD said unto the children of Israel, Ye shall not go in to them, neither shall they come in unto you: for surely they will turn away your heart after their gods: Solomon clave unto these in love.” (KJV)
Read those last words again.
“Solomon clave unto these in love.”
The Hebrew expression is especially revealing.
The text says:
דָּבַק שְׁלֹמֹה לְאַהֲבָה
Dāvaq Shelomoh le'ahavah.
Literally, in its immediate context, Solomon clung to these women in love.
The verb דָּבַק (dāvaq) carries the sense of clinging, holding fast, or attaching oneself closely.

It is a word capable of describing deep covenant attachment. In Genesis 2:24, the same Hebrew verb describes a man cleaving to his wife. In Deuteronomy 10:20, Israel is commanded to hold fast to the LORD.
The word itself is not sinful.
The tragedy lies in the direction of Solomon's attachment.
He clung to relationships that drew his heart away from the God to whom he was commanded to cling.
And that is where this ancient account becomes painfully personal.
Because the greatest spiritual danger is not always something we openly despise.
Sometimes it is something we deeply love.
Something we defend.
Something we cannot imagine surrendering.
Something we keep calling harmless because admitting the truth would require us to change.
And before we continue, we need to understand something essential about this passage.
The problem was not that these women belonged to different ethnic groups.
The biblical warning concerned covenant faithfulness and the danger of being drawn into the worship of other gods.

God's law did not establish a universal prohibition against marriage across ethnic lines. Scripture honors Ruth, a Moabite woman who turned to the LORD and became part of the family line of King David and, ultimately, Jesus Christ.
In Ruth 1:16, she declared:
“Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.” (KJV)
That distinction matters.
Ruth came from a foreign nation, yet embraced Israel's God.
Solomon, by contrast, attached himself to relationships that led him toward foreign gods.
The issue was not ethnicity.
The issue was allegiance.
Deuteronomy 7:3–4 had already warned Israel against marriages with the idolatrous nations in the context of Israel's covenant calling:
“Neither shalt thou make marriages with them…”
And the reason was explicit:
“For they will turn away thy son from following me, that they may serve other gods…”
God was not issuing an arbitrary restriction.
He was identifying a spiritual danger.
The LORD knew what Solomon was choosing to overlook.
And there is a heartbreaking pattern here.
Sometimes God's commandments feel restrictive only because we cannot yet see what His wisdom is protecting us from.
We see the attraction.
God sees the consequence.
We see the immediate satisfaction.
God sees the divided heart.
We see what we are afraid of losing.
God sees what we are in danger of becoming.
And Solomon had more warning than most.
Deuteronomy 17:17 specifically instructed Israel's future king:
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away…”
This was not an obscure warning hidden in a forgotten corner of Scripture.
It addressed the very office Solomon occupied.
Yet First Kings 11:3 tells us he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines.
One thousand women.
An astonishing number.
But the biblical narrator is not merely interested in the size of Solomon's household.
The final words of that verse expose the real catastrophe:
“And his wives turned away his heart.”
There it is.
Not merely his attention.
Not merely his schedule.
Not merely his political priorities.
His heart.
The Hebrew word לֵבָב (lēvāv), translated “heart,” refers to more than emotion. In biblical Hebrew, the heart is central to thought, desire, intention, and moral commitment.
Solomon's downfall was not simply a matter of romantic attachment.
His inner allegiance was being redirected.
And what makes this even more sobering is that the warning was fulfilled exactly as God had said.
First Kings 11:4 records:
“For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods: and his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father.” (KJV)
When Solomon was old.
Those words carry a sadness that is difficult to describe.
He had lived long enough to witness extraordinary answers to prayer.
He had seen the temple completed.
He had witnessed the glory of the LORD fill the house of God.
He had experienced peace, prosperity, influence, and divine generosity.
And still, his heart wandered.
This should silence the assumption that years of religious experience automatically produce spiritual maturity.
You can spend decades around sacred things and still become careless with your soul.
You can know the language of worship and slowly lose the posture of surrender.
You can teach others about wisdom while quietly refusing the wisdom God has already given you.
You can have a history with God and still need to repent today.
And this is where Solomon's story stops feeling ancient.
Because some of us know what it means to make exceptions.
You know that relationship is pulling you away from Christ, but you are afraid of being alone.
You know that private habit is destroying your integrity, but you keep promising yourself it will be the last time.
You know bitterness has been poisoning your prayers, but forgiveness feels too costly.
You know that your ambition has begun to consume the time, honesty, and devotion you once offered freely to God.
You know you are spiritually exhausted because you have been trying to maintain two loyalties that cannot peacefully occupy the same throne.
And still you whisper:
"Just a little longer."
"I can handle it."
"It's not that serious."
"God understands."
God does understand.
But His understanding is not permission to continue in what is destroying us.
His patience is mercy, not approval.
And His warnings are not proof that He wants to steal our joy.
They are evidence that He knows where disobedience leads.
There is another detail in Solomon's story that should make every reader uncomfortable.
His compromise did not remain private.
First Kings 11:5–8 describes Solomon following foreign deities and building high places associated with idolatrous worship.
The man who built a house for the name of the LORD also enabled worship that dishonored the LORD.
Think about the contradiction.
The same hands associated with the construction of the temple became associated with the construction of places for false worship.
A public legacy of devotion stood beside a public legacy of compromise.
And this is why private disobedience must never be dismissed as something that affects only the person committing it.
Sin rarely stays within the boundaries we assign to it.
It reaches marriages.
It reaches children.
It reaches friendships.
It reaches ministries.
It reaches communities.
It changes the example we set and the decisions we make.
What begins as a quiet exception can eventually become something others are invited to accept.
That does not mean every personal struggle will become a public scandal.
But it does mean that the direction of our hearts matters far beyond the moment in which we make a choice.
And perhaps someone reading this has already discovered that.
You did not intend for things to go this far.
You never imagined becoming the person you now struggle to recognize.
You remember when prayer came naturally.
When opening Scripture felt like coming home.
When obedience was not easy, but your desire to honor Jesus was sincere.
Now there are things you avoid thinking about because the truth hurts.
You still believe in God.
But you know there are rooms in your life where you have stopped welcoming His authority.
And you are tired.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of justifying.
Tired of carrying a divided heart into worship and hoping nobody notices.
Listen carefully.
The fact that you are being confronted by Scripture today is an invitation to respond, not a reason to despair.
The story of Solomon is serious because sin is serious.
God's judgment was not imaginary.
First Kings 11:9 tells us that the LORD was angry with Solomon because his heart had turned away from the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice.
And in verses 11–13, God announced that the kingdom would be torn from Solomon's dynasty, though not entirely, because of His covenant commitment concerning David and Jerusalem.
There were consequences.
Real consequences.
Not every broken decision can be reversed.
Not every lost opportunity returns.
Not every wound heals quickly.
And biblical grace does not require us to pretend otherwise.
Yet even within the judgment, God's covenant purposes had not disappeared.
The LORD did not abandon His promise concerning David.
That promise would eventually lead us beyond Solomon to a King greater than Solomon.
And this is where the story begins to turn toward hope.
Because if we stop at Solomon's failure, we will leave with only a warning.
But if we follow the testimony of Scripture to Jesus Christ, we discover something infinitely greater.
In Matthew 12:42, Jesus said:
“And, behold, a greater than Solomon is here.” (KJV)
A greater than Solomon.
Consider what that means.
Solomon received extraordinary wisdom.
Jesus Christ is the One in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Colossians 2:3).
Solomon built a magnificent temple.
Jesus spoke of His own body as the temple that would be raised again (John 2:19–21).
Solomon's heart was turned away through disordered loves.
Jesus loved the Father and obeyed Him perfectly, even to death on the cross.
Solomon's kingdom would be divided.
Christ's kingdom will have no end (Luke 1:33).
Solomon's glory could not save him from the consequences of disobedience.
Christ humbled Himself, bore the judgment due to sinners, and rose again so that those who trust in Him might be forgiven and reconciled to God.
Do you see it?
The answer to Solomon's divided heart is not simply to become more disciplined.
The ultimate answer is to come to the Savior whose heart was never divided.
The King who did not turn away.
The King who obeyed where we have disobeyed.
The King who did not build an altar to false gods, but offered Himself once for sins.
The King who wore a crown of thorns.
The King whose blood was shed for the forgiveness of sinners.
Jesus Christ is not merely a better example than Solomon. He is the Savior Solomon's story teaches us we desperately need.
And this changes everything.
Because perhaps your story already contains decisions you cannot undo.
Perhaps you ignored warnings.
Perhaps you betrayed someone's trust.
Perhaps you compromised what you once defended.
Perhaps you are reading this with tears you would never allow anyone else to see.
And the enemy would love for you to believe that your failure is now your permanent identity.
But the Gospel declares something different.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Not because sin is insignificant.
Not because God has lowered His holiness.
But because Jesus Christ has made forgiveness possible through His sacrifice.
Repentance is not bargaining with God.
It is turning away from sin and turning toward Him.
It is bringing into the light what we have hidden.
It is surrendering what we have defended.
It is refusing to make peace with what Christ died to save us from.
And no, genuine repentance does not mean that every consequence immediately disappears.
But it does mean that sin no longer has to be the master of your life.
Romans 6:14 declares:
“For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace.” (KJV)
Grace does not give us permission to remain enslaved.
Grace calls us into a new life.
And maybe that is the invitation you have been avoiding.
Not another emotional moment that fades by tomorrow.
Not another promise made out of fear.
Not another religious performance designed to cover what is happening inside.
But an actual surrender.
A conversation with God where you stop defending yourself.
Where you admit what you have been clinging to.
Where you ask Him to expose every false loyalty.
Where you finally say:

"Lord Jesus, I have loved things that have pulled my heart away from You. I have made excuses for what You have warned me about. Forgive me. Change my desires. Teach me to love what You love. Give me courage to obey, even when obedience costs me something. I cannot save myself. I trust in Your mercy, Your cross, and Your resurrection. Bring my heart back to You."
And if those words describe what is happening inside you, do not rush past this moment.
Be honest.
What have you been holding on to that is slowly pulling you away from Christ?
Not to perform spirituality for an audience.
But to acknowledge that you need grace, truth, prayer, and a community that will encourage you to keep following Christ.
And please, when you see someone asking for prayer, remember there is a real human being behind those words.
Do not turn their vulnerability into entertainment.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Remind them of Scripture.
Point them toward Jesus.
Because we are not here merely to collect reactions.
We are here to bear witness to the Gospel.
And that is why I want to ask something else of you.
Think of one person who needs to hear this message.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone whose mistakes you want to expose.
Someone you genuinely love.
Maybe a friend who has slowly drifted from church.
A brother who has become discouraged.
A sister carrying secret shame.
A family member who believes they have gone too far to return.
Or someone who has never understood why Jesus came.
Not because every sentence must be remembered.
But because the next time you find yourself rationalizing a compromise, you may need to remember the warning that Solomon ignored.
Knowing the truth is not the same as surrendering to it.
And surrendering to Christ is never a wasted life.
If this message has stirred something in you, I also want to invite you into a deeper journey with Gospel Warrior.
This ministry exists to proclaim Jesus Christ, teach Scripture faithfully, call believers toward repentance, encourage the wounded, and help people grow in the truth of God's Word.
We want these resources to reach believers who cannot afford expensive materials.
We want struggling Christians to find sound biblical encouragement.
We want seekers to encounter the Gospel.
We want families, friends, and entire communities to discover that the Word of God is not merely ancient literature.
It is living truth that points us to the living Christ.
And if this ministry has helped strengthen your faith, you can help us continue and expand that work.

You may choose to give that support as an expression of Christian generosity and stewardship. Scripture encourages believers to support Gospel ministry, while also teaching that giving should be willing rather than pressured.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
But if you believe in this work and are able to support it, your monthly contribution can become one meaningful part of your generosity toward Gospel ministry.
These products are not the reason to follow Jesus.
They are simply an additional expression of appreciation for those who choose to help sustain the work.
Share what strengthens your faith.
Pray for those who are struggling.
Help us make Christ known.
No donation can erase sin.
No ministry can replace Jesus.
Only Christ saves.
And that brings us back to Solomon.
The man who had so much.
The man who knew so much.
The man who had been warned so clearly.
His story asks us to examine what we love, what we obey, and what we are willing to surrender.
Scripture does not explicitly tell us whether Solomon personally repented before his death. We should not invent an ending the biblical text does not give us.
But Scripture does tell us where sinners can find forgiveness.
It tells us of a Savior who receives those who come to Him.
It tells us of a cross where mercy and justice meet.
It tells us of an empty tomb.
It tells us that anyone who is in Christ is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17).
And it tells us that the same Lord who calls us to repent is rich in mercy toward those who trust in Him.
So do not read Solomon's story merely to shake your head at another man's downfall.
Read it with your own heart open before God.
Ask what has been competing for your allegiance.
Ask whether you have been confusing spiritual knowledge with spiritual obedience.
Ask whether the thing you keep defending is worth the distance it is creating between your heart and the Lord.
And then look to Jesus.
Not to your own record.
Not to your reputation.
Not to your ability to fix everything you have broken.
Look to the crucified and risen Christ.
The greater King.
The faithful Savior.
The One who is able to forgive, restore, and transform those who come to Him in faith.
Solomon's story is a warning that even the wisest human heart can wander.
The Gospel is the glorious announcement that Jesus Christ can save wandering sinners.
And perhaps the most important decision you make today will not be something the world ever sees.
It may simply be the moment you stop clinging to what is pulling you away from God…
And begin clinging to Christ.

The most heartbreaking tragedy is not that Solomon had everything and lost his way—it is that we can read his warning, recognize our own divided hearts, and still refuse the hand of Jesus reaching out to bring us home.
